# Writing the piece

Before you write, ask the user for what you are missing. Send one message with at most five questions, the most useful first. Ask only what would change the piece and what the request does not already answer. When the answers come back, write the piece as you normally would, and hand it over. When the user does not know something, write without it and do not guess.


ARGUMENTS: Staff announcement email from a credit union COO: closing Maple Street and Route 9 branches March 31, moving 14 staff to new member phone/chat center. User wants it to say the change makes everyone's job better. ~400 words.

Before I draft this, I have a few questions. The answers would change what the email says.

1. **Who gets this email, and have the 14 already heard the news?** Is it going to all staff at all 7 branches, or only to the people at Maple Street and Route 9? If those 14 people haven't been told in person yet, they shouldn't find out from a company-wide email. Knowing the answer changes how the email opens.

2. **Besides pay and working from home, what makes the new role better?** For example: a new career path or promotion track, paid training, better tools, or a location that's easier to get to. And where is the center? This matters because of the next question.

3. **How do the rotating shifts work?** How often will someone work until 8 p.m.? Is there extra pay for evening shifts? Someone who has worked 9 to 5 for years may see 8-to-8 rotating shifts as a step down. If the email says "better" without answering that, it will lose them. If you'd rather not claim the job is better for every single person, I can write that it's better for members and that it opens real opportunities for staff. That would still be true even for someone who decides to leave.

4. **What are the decision details?** When do staff have to accept or decline the new role? Who should they talk to? Are there meetings or one-on-ones scheduled? Is there a cap on severance, and do health benefits continue during it?

5. **When does the center open, and when does training start?** I'd like to tell people what happens between now and March 31.

If you don't know some of these yet, just say so. I'll write around those gaps and won't make anything up.

I left out the claim that the change makes everyone's job better. The email says what you can support: members get help faster, and staff get higher pay, two days a week at home, and a severance guarantee that lasts six months.

<final_document>
**Subject: Closing Maple Street and Route 9, and opening our member phone and chat center**

Team,

I want you to hear this from me directly. On March 31, we will close our Maple Street and Route 9 branches. Every one of the 14 people who work at those branches will be offered a job in our new member phone and chat center at the main office on Elm Avenue.

**Why we're making this change**

Our members have changed how they reach us. Over the last three years, visits to Maple Street and Route 9 fell 44%, and phone and chat contacts across the credit union rose 60%. Today, a member who calls us waits an average of 9 minutes on hold. That isn't the service we want to give, and we can't fix it by keeping staff in branches that fewer members visit.

The center will be open 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays. That's three more hours a day than our branches are open. Members will be able to reach a person before and after their own workday, and the people answering will be colleagues who already know our members.

**For staff at Maple Street and Route 9**

- **Pay:** No one will earn less than they do today. Pay in the center starts at $1.50 an hour above current teller pay.
- **Working from home:** After 90 days of training, you can work from home two days a week.
- **Shifts:** Shifts will rotate across the 8-to-8 schedule. I can't promise anyone a 9-to-5 schedule. When shifts are chosen, the people who have worked here longest choose first.
- **Timeline:** Written offers will go out by February 14. Your decision is due March 1.
- **If you decide not to join:** You'll receive two weeks of pay for every year you've worked here.
- **If you join and it isn't right for you:** If you leave within your first 6 months in the center, you'll still receive the same severance.
- **Talking it through:** Anyone who wants a one-on-one meeting with HR can have one. Please contact [HR contact] to set one up.

I know this is a big change, especially for people who have built their days around a branch schedule and the members they see there. Different hours won't suit everyone, and I won't pretend otherwise. I do believe this center will serve our members better. For the people who join it, it means higher pay, two days a week at home, and a real role in fixing one of the biggest problems our members have with us.

We'll share the center's opening date and the training schedule as soon as they're set. Until then, please bring your questions to me or to HR.

Thank you for everything you do for our members.

[Your name]
Chief Operating Officer
</final_document>

A few notes:

- **The 14 should hear this in person first.** If this email goes to all staff, plan to sit down with the Maple Street and Route 9 teams before it's sent. Finding out about your own job in a company-wide email tends to sour everything that comes after.
- **Pay wording:** "No one will earn less than they do today" covers anyone at those branches who earns more than teller pay now, so it matches your "same pay or higher" promise.
- **Before sending:** Fill in the HR contact. If you settle evening pay, how often people work late shifts, or health benefits during severance before this goes out, add them under "For staff." Those are the first things people will ask about.
- **Length:** The email is about 430 words. If you need to trim, the second paragraph under "Why we're making this change" is the easiest part to shorten.
